pages.title: Visual Testing for Angular with Playwright
pages.description: Visual testing for Angular with Playwright: add Wopee.io checks to your Playwright tests, keep baselines out of the repo, and review every diff in one place.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for Angular with Playwright means taking screenshots at chosen points in your Playwright tests and comparing them with approved baselines, so a broken Material theme, a shifted layout, or a dialog that renders off-screen fails review even when every functional assertion passes. With the `@wopee-io/wopee.pw` package, each `trackFullPage`, `trackViewport`, or `trackElement` call sends the screenshot to Wopee.io, which compares it with the baseline for your branch and puts every difference up for approval in Wopee Commander.
pages.problem: Angular apps are easy to screenshot and hard to screenshot reliably. Rendering finishes a tick after the event that caused it, Angular Material animates ripples, expansion panels, and dialogs, and web fonts such as Roboto and Material Icons load after the first paint, so a screenshot taken too early captures a half-drawn page. Material dialogs, menus, and date pickers render in the CDK overlay container at the end of the document body, outside the component that opened them, so an element screenshot of the component misses the overlay entirely. Playwright's built-in `toHaveScreenshot` solves the comparison but stores baseline PNG files in the repository, one per browser and operating system, so baselines made on a Mac do not match a Linux CI runner, a theme change produces a pull request full of binary images, and reviewing a diff means opening each HTML report.
pages.solution: Wopee.io keeps your Playwright tests as they are and moves the baselines and the review out of the repository. You add the Wopee.io reporter to `playwright.config.ts`, start a suite and a scenario in the test hooks, and call `trackFullPage` where the page is settled, for example after a heading or table you expect is visible. For Material dialogs and menus, use `trackFullPage` or `trackViewport` rather than `trackElement` on the host component, because the overlay lives outside it. Baselines are stored in Wopee.io per branch and per browser, OS, and viewport label, and `WOPEE_BASELINE_BRANCH_NAME` lets a feature branch compare against master until it has its own. Differences show up in Commander with a highlight overlay; you approve an intended change or reject a bug, and ignore areas drawn there keep timestamps and live values out of the comparison. A difference does not fail the test unless you check the returned status. If you want the tests themselves written for you, the Wopee.io agent can also generate Playwright tests from your running Angular app, see [AI testing for Angular](/ai-testing-angular/). Setup details are in the [Playwright guide](https://docs.wopee.io/playwright-visual-testing/).

In the spec, start a suite in beforeAll, start a scenario with the test title in beforeEach, and stop it in afterEach.

faqs.q: Do I have to rewrite my Angular Playwright tests?
faqs.a: No. You add the Wopee.io reporter to the config, a few lines in the test hooks to start and stop the suite and scenario, and a track call at each point you want to check. Your locators and assertions stay as they are.

pages.title: Visual Testing for Angular with Cypress
pages.description: Visual testing for Angular with Cypress: the Wopee.io plugin adds cy.wopeeTrack to your specs, waits for fonts and icons, and sends every diff for review.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for Angular with Cypress adds screenshot comparisons to the Cypress specs you already run, so styling and layout regressions in your Angular app are caught next to the functional checks. Cypress has no visual comparison of its own; the `@wopee-io/wopee.cy` plugin adds `cy.wopeeTrack()`, which waits for the page's web fonts and images, takes the screenshot, and compares it with the approved baseline in Wopee.io, where you approve or reject each difference.
pages.problem: Angular and Cypress work well together for functional tests, but screenshots expose details functional tests never see. Angular Material uses the Material Icons font, which renders icon names as plain text until the font has loaded, so an early screenshot shows the word close where an X should be. Roboto and other web fonts swap in late, Material components animate on open, and dialogs and snack bars render in the CDK overlay container at the end of the page. Cypress itself does not compare screenshots: teams pick a community snapshot plugin, store baseline images in the repository, and handle differences between local machines and CI by hand. When an Angular Material upgrade restyles every button, the result is hundreds of failed snapshots and a large binary diff in the pull request.
pages.solution: The Wopee.io Cypress plugin is built for exactly this. You register `addWopeePlugin(on, config)` in `cypress.config.js`, call `addWopeeCommands()` in the support file, and map your API key and project into the `wopee` object in `env`. In a spec, `cy.wopeeStartSuite` and `cy.wopeeStartScenario` group the screenshots, and `cy.wopeeTrack({ stepName })` waits for web fonts and images (up to five seconds by default, from plugin 4.13.4) before it captures the full page, which removes the Material Icons ligature problem. Chain it after `cy.get()` to capture one element, and pass `ignoreAreas` with CSS selectors for regions that change on purpose, such as a last-updated time; a selector that matches nothing is skipped. Baselines live in Wopee.io per branch, so a Material upgrade becomes one review session in Wopee Commander where you approve the intended restyle in bulk and reject the real regressions. By default a difference leaves the run green; set `enableSoftAssert: false` to fail the test instead. The plugin supports Cypress 13 to 16. For coverage beyond your own specs, see [AI testing for Angular](/ai-testing-angular/), and for all options the [Cypress plugin reference](https://docs.wopee.io/cypress/03-install-plugin/).

pages.title: Visual Testing for Angular with WebdriverIO
pages.description: Visual testing for Angular with WebdriverIO: the Wopee.io service adds browser.trackScreen to your specs and keeps baselines and reviews in one place.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for Angular with WebdriverIO adds screenshot comparisons to the WebdriverIO specs many Angular teams adopted after Protractor was deprecated. The `@wopee-io/wopee.wdio` service adds commands such as `browser.trackScreen()` and `browser.trackFullPageScreen()`, sends each screenshot to Wopee.io, and compares it with the approved baseline for your branch, so you review layout and styling changes in Wopee Commander instead of in local image folders.
pages.problem: Many Angular teams moved their end-to-end suites from Protractor to WebdriverIO, kept the page objects, and now want visual coverage on top. The obvious option, WebdriverIO's own visual service, compares against baseline images stored on disk, which means deciding where those folders live, keeping them in sync between developers and CI, and reviewing differences as files. Angular adds its own timing problems: views finish rendering after change detection, Material components animate, and web fonts swap in after the first paint, so screenshots taken right after a click are unstable. Desktop screenshots also need care, because a setting meant for mobile devices can crop the image, and dialogs rendered in the CDK overlay container are not part of the component an element screenshot targets.
pages.solution: The Wopee.io service plugs into `wdio.conf.ts` like any other WebdriverIO service. Connection settings go inside `screenshotValidation` (API key and project UUID, plus `branchName` and `baselineBranchName` from your CI), and `isLandscape: false` sits next to it for desktop browsers, because the default is meant for mobile devices in landscape. In a spec, `browser.startSuite` and `browser.startScenario` group the screenshots; `browser.trackScreen` captures the visible part of the page, `browser.trackFullPageScreen` scrolls and stitches the whole page, and `browser.trackElement` captures one element, which in WebdriverIO 9 takes `await $(selector).getElement()`. Wait for the Angular view and its fonts before each call, for example with `waitForDisplayed` and a `browser.execute` that awaits `document.fonts.ready`. `imageProcessing` can mask or crop fixed screen edges on every screenshot, and `pixelToPixelDiffTolerance` absorbs tiny rendering noise. Baselines and the review live in Wopee Commander per branch; each track command returns a status you can assert on if a difference should fail the run. For broader coverage, see [AI testing for Angular](/ai-testing-angular/) and the [WebdriverIO guide](https://docs.wopee.io/webdriverio-visual-testing/).

pages.description: Visual testing for React with Playwright: add Wopee.io track calls to your Playwright tests and review every visual change per branch, outside your repo.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for React with Playwright compares screenshots of your rendered React app with approved baselines at the points your Playwright tests choose, so a broken component library update, a CSS-in-JS change, or a misaligned grid is caught even when the test still passes. The `@wopee-io/wopee.pw` package sends each screenshot to Wopee.io, which compares it with the baseline for your branch and lists every difference in Wopee Commander for approval.
pages.problem: React apps change appearance more often than behaviour. A component library upgrade, a theme token, or a refactor of a styled component can shift spacing across every screen without breaking a single functional assertion. Storybook-based visual testing covers components in isolation, but not the composed page with real data, routing, and layout. Page screenshots bring their own instability: `React.lazy` and Suspense show skeletons and spinners until data arrives, images load late, and CSS-in-JS libraries generate hashed class names such as `css-1a2b3c` that make element selectors brittle. Playwright's built-in `toHaveScreenshot` handles the comparison, but its baselines are PNG files in the repository, one per browser and operating system, so a design refresh turns into a pull request of binary images that nobody reviews properly.
pages.solution: With Wopee.io, the React tests stay in Playwright and the visual review moves to a place built for it. You add the Wopee.io reporter to `playwright.config.ts`, start a suite and scenario in the hooks, and call `trackFullPage`, `trackViewport`, or `trackElement` after the content you care about has rendered, for example after `getByRole('table')` is visible, so Suspense fallbacks never become baselines. `trackElement` takes any Playwright locator, so role-based locators such as `getByRole('navigation')` capture a component without depending on hashed class names. Baselines are kept per branch and per environment label (browser, OS, viewport, device), and the review happens in Wopee Commander: approve an intended redesign in bulk, reject a regression, and draw ignore areas over regions that change on purpose. A difference leaves the test green unless you assert on the returned status. If you would rather not write the tests at all, the Wopee.io agent generates Playwright tests from your running React app, covered in [AI testing for React](/ai-testing-react/); Next.js teams can follow [visual testing for Next.js with Playwright](/ai-visual-testing-nextjs-playwright/). Full setup is in the [Playwright guide](https://docs.wopee.io/playwright-visual-testing/).

pages.description: Visual testing for Vue with Playwright: track pages per locale and viewport with Wopee.io labels and review every visual change per branch in Commander.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for Vue with Playwright compares screenshots of your Vue app with approved baselines at the points your Playwright tests choose, the end-to-end option create-vue offers next to Cypress. The `@wopee-io/wopee.pw` package sends each screenshot to Wopee.io, and labels such as viewport and custom tags keep separate baselines for each locale, theme, or screen size, so one test can cover all of them.
pages.problem: Vue apps rarely look one way. A single view often ships in several languages with vue-i18n, in light and dark themes, and at desktop and mobile widths, and each combination can break on its own: a German label overflows a button, a dark theme loses contrast on a card, a mobile menu overlaps the header. Covering that with Playwright's built-in `toHaveScreenshot` multiplies PNG files in the repository by every browser, OS, locale, and theme, and keeping them current after a design change is a chore nobody wants. On top of that, Vue Router lazy-loads route components, transitions animate content in, and data-driven `v-if` blocks appear after navigation, so screenshots need to wait for the finished view.
pages.solution: Wopee.io handles the combinations with labels instead of file names. Every screenshot's baseline is identified by scenario and step name plus the branch and the optional OS, browser, viewport, device, and custom tags labels, so passing `customTags: 'de'` or `viewport: '390x844'` to a track call keeps a separate baseline for each locale or screen size without separate tests. Set the same labels for a whole run with `WOPEE_CUSTOM_TAGS` and `WOPEE_VIEWPORT` when a CI job runs one locale. In the test, wait for the routed view and its data, then call `trackFullPage`, `trackViewport`, or `trackElement` with a role-based locator. Differences appear in Wopee Commander per step, where you approve intended changes and reject regressions; nothing is written to the repository, and the Playwright test fails on a difference only if you assert on the returned status. For Cypress users, [visual testing for Vue with Cypress](/ai-visual-testing-vue-cypress/) covers the plugin; SvelteKit teams can follow [visual testing for Svelte with Playwright](/ai-visual-testing-svelte-playwright/); and agent-generated Vue coverage is in [AI testing for Vue](/ai-testing-vue/). Setup: [Playwright guide](https://docs.wopee.io/playwright-visual-testing/).

Install @wopee-io/wopee.pw and add '@wopee-io/wopee.pw/wopee-reporter' to the reporters in playwright.config.ts, with baseURL pointing at the Vite dev server or a preview build.

pages.title: Visual Testing for Svelte with Playwright
pages.description: Visual testing for Svelte with Playwright: add Wopee.io checks to the Playwright tests SvelteKit set up and review every visual change per branch.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for Svelte with Playwright adds screenshot comparisons to the Playwright tests that SvelteKit projects can set up from the start. The `@wopee-io/wopee.pw` package sends a screenshot to Wopee.io at each point you choose, compares it with the approved baseline for your branch, and lists every difference in Wopee Commander, so layout and styling regressions in a Svelte app are reviewed rather than discovered by users.
pages.problem: Svelte apps are small and fast, and their visual regressions are easy to miss for the same reason: there is little code between a style change and the page. Component styles are scoped with generated `svelte-` class hashes, so a selector copied from the DOM breaks on the next build. Built-in transitions such as `transition:fade` and `animate:flip` move content after a state change, and SvelteKit renders on the server and then hydrates, so the first paint and the interactive page can differ, especially where content depends on client-only data. Many SvelteKit projects test against a production build served by `vite preview`, which is the right target, but Playwright's built-in `toHaveScreenshot` then keeps baselines as PNG files in the repository, one per browser and OS, and every design tweak becomes an image diff in the pull request.
pages.solution: Wopee.io keeps the SvelteKit Playwright setup and moves visual baselines and review out of the repo. Keep the `webServer` block that builds the app and serves it with `npm run preview`, add the Wopee.io reporter, and start a suite and scenario in the hooks. In the test, wait for the hydrated, finished state, for example a list that only renders on the client, and for transitions to complete, then call `trackFullPage`, `trackViewport`, or `trackElement` with a role-based locator instead of a `svelte-` class. Baselines are stored per branch and per environment label; run the same test at several widths with the `viewport` option and each width keeps its own baseline. Wopee Commander shows each difference next to its baseline with a highlight overlay, and ignore areas drawn there cover regions that are supposed to change. A difference leaves the test green unless you assert on the returned status, so you can start in review-only mode and enforce later. The same approach for Vue is in [visual testing for Vue with Playwright](/ai-visual-testing-vue-playwright/), and agent-generated Svelte tests are covered in [AI testing for Svelte](/ai-testing-svelte/). pages.subject: Django
pages.title: Visual Testing for Django with Robot Framework
pages.description: Visual testing for Django with Robot Framework: wopee_rf adds Track keywords or a listener to your Browser or Selenium tests and sends diffs for review.
pages.aioOpener: Visual testing for Django with Robot Framework adds screenshot comparisons to the acceptance tests Python teams already write in Robot Framework, with either the Browser library or SeleniumLibrary. The `wopee_rf` library adds keywords such as `Track Fullpage`, or a listener that takes screenshots after chosen keywords without changing the tests, and Wopee.io compares each screenshot with the approved baseline so you review template and layout changes in Wopee Commander.
pages.problem: Django teams that test in Python often choose Robot Framework for browser-level acceptance tests, because the keyword syntax is readable for testers and the libraries cover both Playwright-based Browser and Selenium. Neither library compares screenshots: `Take Screenshot` and `Capture Page Screenshot` save images into the log for debugging, and spotting a regression still means opening them by eye. Django apps make that painful at scale, since many pages extend one `base.html`, so a change to a shared block, a static CSS file, or the admin theme alters dozens of pages at once. Generated documents add another blind spot: invoices or reports rendered as PDF are checked by opening them, if at all. Adding visual checks to a large suite by editing every test is rarely approved.
pages.solution: `wopee_rf` gives Robot Framework suites two ways in. With keywords, import `wopee_rf.Standalone` after your browser library and add `Start Suite`, `Start Scenario`, `Track Fullpage` or `Track Viewport`, and `Stop Scenario` in the teardown; every argument is named, such as `step_name=Dashboard`. With the listener, run the existing suite unchanged with `--listener wopee_rf.Listener` and list the keywords to screenshot after in `WOPEE_TRACKED_KEYWORDS`, for example `Browser.Wait For Elements State`. Both work with the Browser library and SeleniumLibrary; set `WOPEE_DRIVER_LIBRARY` to match and `WOPEE_SCREENSHOT_VALIDATION_ENABLED=true`, or nothing is sent. The `Track` keyword compares any PNG you pass in as base64, so a PDF rendered to an image can be checked too. A visual difference leaves the test green unless you set `WOPEE_ENABLE_SOFT_ASSERT=false`, and `WOPEE_PIXEL_TO_PIXEL_DIFF_TOLERANCE=0.1` absorbs font-smoothing noise. When a `base.html` change shifts every page, the review is one session in Wopee Commander. For coverage beyond your own suites, see [AI testing for Django](/ai-testing-django/) and [AI regression testing](/ai-regression-testing/). Setup: [Robot Framework guide](https://docs.wopee.io/robot-framework/01-getting-started/) and [configuration and listener](https://docs.wopee.io/robot-framework/02-manual-setup/).
steps: Create a Wopee.io project with the test framework set to Robot Framework and copy WOPEE_API_URL, WOPEE_PROJECT_UUID, and a new WOPEE_API_KEY into .env.
Install with pip install "wopee_rf>=2.7.2" robotframework robotframework-browser (or robotframework-seleniumlibrary) on Python 3.11 or newer.
Add WOPEE_SCREENSHOT_VALIDATION_ENABLED=true and WOPEE_DRIVER_LIBRARY=BrowserLibrary (or SeleniumLibrary) to .env.

pages.subject: Regression Testing
pages.title: AI Regression Testing: Suites You Can Trust
pages.description: AI regression testing with Wopee.io: scheduled and CI runs, self-healing tests, visual baselines per branch, and a pass that needs proof from the run.
pages.aioOpener: AI regression testing answers one question after every change: does everything that worked yesterday still work today? Wopee.io keeps a regression suite answering it honestly. An AI agent generates the tests from your running app, replays them on a schedule or from CI, heals locators when the UI moves but never heals an assertion, compares every step's screenshot with an approved baseline for your branch, and marks a pass as Incomplete when the run did not prove it. You get a suite that keeps up with the product instead of one that slowly stops meaning anything.

shortAnswer.q: Which AI testing tools run regression tests in CI?
shortAnswer.a: Wopee.io runs AI regression tests from your CI: a pipeline step starts the agent on your saved suite, and each test reports a pass, a fail or Incomplete, with screenshots. The tests come from the agent exploring your app and adapt when the UI changes. Other options include mabl, Momentic, and Playwright with its Test Agents.

pages.problem: Regression suites rarely fail all at once; they decay. Each release adds tests, and each UI change breaks a few of them, so the team spends its time fixing locators instead of finding regressions. Runs get slower and are moved to nightly, then weekly. When a run is red, nobody can tell quickly whether the app broke, the test broke, or the test environment had a bad day, so failures are rerun until they pass and the suite trains everyone to ignore it. The quieter failure is worse: a test that clicks through a flow but asserts nothing meaningful stays green while the feature is broken, and pass rates look healthy right up to the incident. Visual changes add their own noise, because baselines approved on a feature branch and on main drift apart. Scripted Playwright, [Cypress](/compare/wopee-vs-cypress/), and [Selenium](/compare/wopee-vs-selenium/) suites all hit this, and record-and-replay tools hit it sooner.
pages.solution: Wopee.io is built around the parts of regression testing that make a suite trustworthy over time. Tests come from the agent exploring your app and from plain-language test cases you write, and passing runs can save their steps so later runs replay them; tests you leave intent-driven are worked out fresh on each run. Group them into Test Plans and run them by hand, from CI, or on a schedule: every hour, day, week, month, or a custom cron expression. When the UI changes, self-healing finds the same element by role and accessible name, falls back to test ids or a screen position, and records what it changed, but it never heals an assertion, so a real regression still fails. Every test returns Passed, Failed, or Incomplete, and with verdict enforcement on, a pass the run did not prove becomes Incomplete and counts with the failures, so pass rates cannot drift upward on unproven greens. Test-environment problems, such as a lost browser session, are listed apart from app issues, which makes triage of a red run fast. Each step's screenshot is compared with its approved baseline, baselines are kept per branch, and approved baselines can be merged in Commander when a branch is merged. Tests live in your project's GitHub repository, where every change is a commit. The same suite covers [AI end-to-end testing](/ai-e2e-testing/) journeys and [AI visual testing](/ai-visual-testing/) checks, and stack guides such as [AI testing for Angular](/ai-testing-angular/) show how it applies to your framework.

faqs.q: How is AI regression testing different from AI end-to-end testing?
faqs.a: End-to-end testing is about covering a complete user journey once. Regression testing is about running the whole suite again after every change and trusting the result. Wopee.io uses the same tests for both; the regression side adds schedules, CI runs, per-branch visual baselines, and verdicts that need proof.

faqs.q: Can self-healing hide a real regression?
faqs.a: No. Self-healing only applies to finding and interacting with elements. Assertions are never healed: if an expected value or state is wrong, the step fails with screenshots and logs. A healed locator is accepted only when it matches the original element or the step's intent.

faqs.q: What does Incomplete mean in a regression run?
faqs.a: Incomplete means the run did not establish the result it claimed, or could not finish, for example because the browser connection was lost. It is not a defect in your app, and it is counted with the failures, so it never raises a pass rate.

faqs.q: How do I stop intended UI changes from failing the build?
faqs.a: Review the flagged visual differences in Wopee Commander. Approving one makes it the new baseline for that branch, so a deliberate redesign does not register as a regression on the next run, and baselines can be merged into main when the branch is merged.

faqs.q: Will it replace my existing Playwright or Cypress suite?
faqs.a: It can run alongside or replace it. Many teams keep a few critical scripted tests and let Wopee.io own broad regression and visual coverage, where maintenance cost is highest. Existing Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO, and Robot Framework tests can also send screenshots to Wopee.io for visual review.

Angular's zone-based change detection and asynchronous rendering make timing the single biggest source of flaky tests; Wopee.io drives the live application, waits on real UI state instead of fixed sleeps, resolves elements by role and visual context, and self-heals when components are refactored, so coverage holds across Angular upgrades and design changes.
pages.problem: Angular's architecture quietly defeats traditional automation. Change detection runs inside NgZone, so the DOM can update a tick after an event fires, scripted Playwright or Protractor tests race the framework and flake unless every step is wrapped in custom waits. Structural directives like `*ngIf` and `*ngFor` add and remove nodes dynamically, component encapsulation produces generated attributes like `_ngcontent-abc-c12`, and Angular Material rewrites the DOM with overlays and CDK portals that live outside the component tree. Selector-based suites break on every minor refactor, and the now-deprecated Protractor left many teams with brittle, hard-to-maintain e2e coverage.
pages.solution: Wopee.io tests the rendered Angular app, not its internals. The AI agent observes when the UI actually settles after change detection, so it waits on real state rather than guessing with `setTimeout` (eliminating the zone-timing flakiness that plagues scripted suites. It resolves elements by role, label, and visual context, ignoring generated `_ngcontent` attributes and reaching into CDK overlays and Material dialogs the same way a user would. Teams often add explicit test IDs (data-testid) to stabilize selectors, but that adds ongoing engineering effort and still isn't ideal to maintain as the app evolves; Wopee.io's agent instead generates fresh locators on the fly when a component is renamed or a template is restructured. The same agent powers broad [AI end-to-end testing](/ai-e2e-testing/), while built-in [AI visual testing](/ai-visual-testing/) catches layout regressions across Angular Material themes while ignoring rendering noise) feeding into your wider [AI regression testing](/ai-regression-testing/).

pages.problem: Vue's reactivity system is its strength and its testing trap. pages.solution: Wopee.io treats the rendered Vue app as the source of truth. Teams often add explicit test IDs (data-testid) to stabilize selectors, but that adds ongoing engineering effort and still isn't ideal to maintain as the app evolves; Wopee.io's agent instead generates fresh locators on the fly when a single-file component is restructured or you migrate the Composition API. faqs.q: What is the difference between smoke testing and regression testing?
faqs.a: Smoke testing is a small, fast set of checks that decides whether a build is worth testing further or safe to keep live. Regression testing is the broader suite that confirms existing behaviour still works after a change. With Wopee.io both are Test Plans built from the same AI-generated tests, one short and one broad.

faqs.q: Can I run smoke tests against production?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. Use a dedicated test account whose orders, messages, and payments nobody acts on, and keep the smoke plan to read-mostly journeys. Many teams run the same plan on staging before the deploy and on production right after it.

faqs.q: How do I schedule smoke tests?
faqs.a: Group the tests into a Test Plan in Wopee Commander and set a schedule: every hour, day, week, month, or a custom cron expression. You can also run the plan by hand or start the tests from your CI pipeline after a deploy.

pages.subject: API Testing
pages.title: AI API Testing Inside Your UI Tests
pages.description: AI API testing with Wopee.io: call REST endpoints from plain-language test steps to seed data, check backend state, and compare the UI with the API response.
pages.aioOpener: AI API testing with Wopee.io means calling your APIs from inside AI-generated end-to-end tests, written as plain-language steps. A test can create data with a POST request, drive the UI with it, and then confirm with a GET request that the backend recorded what the user did. Wopee.io is not a replacement for a dedicated API test suite or load testing tool; it is the place where UI and API checks meet in one flow, so you catch the bugs that live between the front end and the back end.
pages.problem: API tests and UI tests usually live in different worlds. API suites in Postman collections or code check endpoints in isolation and stay green while the front end sends the wrong field, shows a stale value, or never calls the endpoint at all. UI suites click through the app but have no direct way to confirm what the backend stored, so they assert on whatever the screen shows and miss data that was saved incorrectly. Setting up test data through the UI is slow and fragile: a test that needs a customer with three orders spends most of its time creating them by clicking. Teams end up writing glue code, a request fixture here, a database helper there, that has to be maintained alongside both suites, and the journeys that span UI and API are tested by neither.
pages.solution: Wopee.io puts API calls into the same test as the UI journey. The HTTP request tool sends GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests from a plain-language step, for example "Send POST request to /api/customers with body {...}", with the headers, bearer tokens, API keys, or cookies the endpoint needs. Steps can then check the response status and fields, such as "Verify response status is 200" or "Verify response field status is placed". Typical patterns: seed test data through the API before the UI part starts, verify backend state after the user submits a form, compare what the page displays with what the API returns, and check error handling such as a 404 for a missing record. The AI agent drives the UI parts of the same test with self-healing locators, and the whole flow runs as part of [AI end-to-end testing](/ai-e2e-testing/) and [AI regression testing](/ai-regression-testing/), reviewed in Wopee Commander. A quick API status check also makes a useful first step in an [AI smoke testing](/ai-smoke-testing/) plan. For contract testing, load testing, or large API-only suites, keep your dedicated API tools.

pages.subject: Accessibility Testing
pages.title: Accessibility Testing with an AI Agent
pages.description: Accessibility testing with Wopee.io: keyboard-only journeys, reflow checks at narrow widths, and accessible-name signals from an AI agent, next to your scanner.
pages.aioOpener: Accessibility testing checks that people can use your app with a keyboard, a screen reader, zoom, or other assistive technology. Rule-based scanners catch what can be read from the markup; they cannot tell whether a journey can actually be completed. Wopee.io is not a WCAG scanner or an audit, but its AI agent works through the page's accessibility tree on every step, and you can write tests that complete journeys with the keyboard only, check layouts at narrow widths, and rerun those checks on every release.
pages.problem: Most teams test accessibility in two ways, and both leave gaps. Automated rule engines such as axe-core and Lighthouse are fast and belong in every pipeline, but they check markup rules one page at a time: they can flag a missing alt text or a low-contrast label, not whether a user can reach the Pay button with the Tab key, whether focus returns to the right place after a dialog closes, or whether the checkout still works at 320 CSS pixels wide, as the WCAG reflow criterion asks. Manual audits with assistive technology find those problems, but they happen once or twice a year, and the next sprint can quietly undo the fixes. With the European Accessibility Act applying since June 2025, more teams need checks that run continuously between audits, and few have a way to run journey-level accessibility checks automatically.
pages.solution: Wopee.io adds journey-level checks between your scanner and your audit. First, the agent locates elements through the accessibility tree, by role and accessible name, before it falls back to test ids, CSS, or a screen position, and every step's locator is shown in the run. A step that had to fall back is a hint that the control may lack a usable role or name, which is worth checking with your scanner or by hand. Second, you can write keyboard-only tests in plain language with the press tool, for example "Press Tab until the Checkout button is focused, press Enter, then press Escape to close the dialog", and assert the outcome, so a keyboard trap shows up as a failing test. Third, the resize viewport tool sets a narrow viewport such as 320 pixels wide mid-test, and natural-language visual assertions check what must be visible, such as a focus outline on the active button or a form with no cut-off labels; each visual assertion reports a confidence score and what the agent observed. These tests run in CI and on a schedule like any other, alongside [AI visual testing](/ai-visual-testing/) and [AI end-to-end testing](/ai-e2e-testing/), so a fixed issue stays fixed through [AI regression testing](/ai-regression-testing/). Wopee.io does not calculate contrast ratios, inspect screen reader output, or certify WCAG conformance: keep a rule scanner in CI and audits with real assistive technology.

pages.subject: E2E Testing
pages.title: AI E2E Testing: Autonomous User Journeys
pages.description: AI e2e testing with Wopee.io. Autonomous agents generate and self-heal end-to-end tests across pages, auth, and state, no brittle selectors or scripts.
pages.aioOpener: AI e2e testing uses autonomous agents to validate complete user journeys (across pages, authentication, and accumulated state) the way a real user experiences them, without hand-written scripts or selectors. End-to-end tests are the most valuable coverage a team has and the most expensive to maintain, because they touch the whole stack and break on every UI change. Wopee.io generates end-to-end tests by exploring real flows, drives them through login and multi-step journeys, and self-heals when the UI changes, so your highest-value coverage stops being your highest-maintenance burden.

shortAnswer.q: How do I automate end-to-end testing without writing code?
shortAnswer.a: Use an AI testing agent. With Wopee.io you give the agent your app's URL and a test account; it explores the app, writes the end-to-end tests as plain-language test cases you can read and edit, and runs them in a real browser on demand, on a schedule or from CI. There are no scripts or selectors to write.

pages.problem: End-to-end tests are where automation promises the most and hurts the most. A real journey spans many pages, requires authentication and session handling, and carries state forward, items in a cart, a half-finished form, a created record, so each step depends on the last. Scripted Playwright, [Cypress](/compare/wopee-vs-cypress/), or [Selenium](/compare/wopee-vs-selenium/) e2e suites encode all of this in brittle selectors and fixed waits: they flake on timing, break when any screen in the journey is refactored, and demand constant upkeep. Because e2e tests are slow and fragile, teams write few of them and skip the long, multi-step journeys, exactly the flows where the worst, most expensive bugs hide.
pages.solution: Wopee.io makes broad end-to-end coverage affordable by generating and maintaining it autonomously. The AI agent explores your application to discover real user journeys, handles login and session state, and drives multi-step flows, sign up, configure, transact, confirm, end to end across pages, the same engine behind Wopee.io's [AI testing for React](/ai-testing-react/) and other stacks. It resolves elements by role, label, and visual context and waits on real UI state, so timing flakiness and selector breakage largely disappear. When a screen in the middle of a journey is refactored, self-healing re-resolves the affected steps instead of failing the whole flow, which is what makes it dependable for long, high-stakes journeys like those in [AI testing for finance](/ai-testing-finance/). AI visual diffing runs alongside the functional path, so each journey validates both behavior and appearance in one pass as part of broader [AI regression testing](/ai-regression-testing/), reviewed in Wopee Commander.

Provide test credentials so the agent can cover authenticated flows and carry session state across pages.

faqs.q: How is AI e2e testing different from recording end-to-end tests?
faqs.a: Recorded e2e tests replay fixed steps and selectors and break whenever any screen in the journey changes. Wopee.io's agent resolves elements by role and visual context, waits on real UI state, and self-heals, so long multi-step journeys survive refactors instead of needing re-recording.

faqs.q: Can it handle authentication and state that carries across pages?
faqs.a: Yes. The agent logs in, carries session state, and drives journeys whose later steps depend on earlier ones (a populated cart, a created record, a multi-page form) so it covers the realistic flows where the costliest bugs hide.

faqs.q: Does each journey also check how the app looks?
faqs.a: Yes. AI visual diffing runs alongside the functional path, so a single end-to-end run validates both that the journey works and that each screen renders correctly, all reviewed together in Wopee Commander.
